title: Vector helpers
text:
Vector helpers are evaluated once per group on whole columns. Use them as mutate(), filter(), and summarize() arguments. They follow R’s NA rules: a summary returns NA when its input has an NA unless naRm: true, ranks keep NA, and cumulative functions stay NA after the first NA.
The first argument is the input column. A string there is a column name. It can also be col('x'), another helper, or a row closure. Later arguments are values. ->map(fn ($value, $r) => ...) transforms a helper’s result row by row.

title: Vector helpers
text:
Window functions







Helper
Value




lag('x', n:, default:, orderBy:), lead(...)
Shifted values


row_number(), row_number('x')
Row numbers, or ranks with ties broken by position


min_rank, dense_rank
Ranks; wrap the column in desc() to reverse


percent_rank, cume_dist
Ranks scaled to [0, 1]


ntile('x', 4)
Buckets of near-equal size


cumsum, cumprod, cummin, cummax, cummean
Running values


cumall, cumany
Running logical values


consecutive_id('x')
A new id each time the value changes


order_by('t', cumsum('x'))
A window function evaluated in another order




PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


// Female Chinstrap penguins, from the shortest flippers up.
echo DataFrame::fromCsv("$data/penguins.csv") |>
    filter(fn ($r) => $r->species === 'Chinstrap' && $r->sex === 'female') |>
    arrange('flipper_length_mm') |>
    mutate(
        prev: lag('body_mass_g'),
        change: lag('body_mass_g')->map(fn ($prev, $r) => $prev === null ? null : $r->body_mass_g - $prev),
        running_mean: cummean('body_mass_g'),
        rank: min_rank(desc('body_mass_g')),
        pct: percent_rank('body_mass_g'),
        quartile: ntile('body_mass_g', 4),
    ) |>
    select('flipper_length_mm', 'body_mass_g', 'prev', 'change', 'running_mean', 'rank', 'pct', 'quartile') |>
    head(8);


// Female Chinstrap penguins, from the shortest flippers up.

title: Vector helpers
text:
Conditionals and NA







Helper
Use




if_else(cond, yes, no, missing:)
Vectorized if/else


case_when([cond, value], ..., default:)
The first true condition wins


replace_when('x', [cond, value], ...)
case_when() that keeps x where nothing matches


recode_values('x', [from, to], ..., default:)
Map values; also from: / to: lookup lists


replace_values('x', [from, to], ...)
recode_values() that keeps unmatched values


case_match('x', [from, to], ..., default:)
dplyr’s deprecated form of recode_values()


recode('x', a: 'A', _default:, _missing:)
dplyr’s superseded recoder, matching values by name


when_any(...), when_all(...)
Elementwise OR and AND across conditions


coalesce('x', 0)
The first non-NA value


na_if('x', value)
NA where x equals the value


between('x', lo, hi)
Inclusive range test


near('x', y)
Equality within floating-point tolerance




PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


echo DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['state' => 'NC', 'visits' => 3],
    ['state' => 'NYC', 'visits' => null],
    ['state' => 'CA', 'visits' => 12],
    ['state' => null, 'visits' => 0],
]) |>
    mutate(
        name: recode_values('state', ['NC', 'North Carolina'], [['NY', 'NYC'], 'New York'], default: 'other'),
        visits: coalesce('visits', 0),
        busy: if_else(fn ($r) => $r->visits > 5, 'yes', 'no'),
        capped: replace_when('visits', [fn ($r) => $r->visits > 10, 10]),
        any_flag: when_any(fn ($r) => $r->state === 'CA', fn ($r) => $r->visits === 0),
    );


echo phplyr(DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['state' => 'NC', 'visits' => 3],
    ['state' => 'NYC', 'visits' => null],
    ['state' => 'CA', 'visits' => 12],
    ['state' => null, 'visits' => 0],
]))
    ->mutate(
        name: recode_values('state', ['NC', 'North Carolina'], [['NY', 'NYC'], 'New York'], default: 'other'),
        visits: coalesce('visits', 0),
        busy: if_else(fn ($r) => $r->visits > 5, 'yes', 'no'),
        capped: replace_when('visits', [fn ($r) => $r->visits > 10, 10]),
        any_flag: when_any(fn ($r) => $r->state === 'CA', fn ($r) => $r->visits === 0),
    );

if_else()
if_else(mixed $condition, mixed $true, mixed $false, mixed $missing = null): Vec
Vectorised if/else. A null condition gives $missing.
Returns a vector helper (Vec). Its expression runs on a database table when its arguments are columns, literals, or other helpers. Example.


case_when()
case_when(mixed ...$cases): Vec
The value of the first case whose condition is true, else $default. Cases are [condition, value] pairs: case_when([fn ($r) => $r->x < 0, 'neg'], [fn ($r) => $r->x > 0, 'pos'], default: 'zero').
Returns a vector helper (Vec). Its expression runs on a database table when its arguments are columns, literals, or other helpers. Throws InvalidArgumentException on invalid arguments.


case_match()
case_match(mixed $x, mixed ...$cases): Vec
Match values like a switch (deprecated in dplyr 1.2 in favor of recode_values()): case_match('code', [['a', 'b'], 'vowel'], ['z', 'last'], default: 'other').
Returns a vector helper (Vec). Its expression runs on a database table when its arguments are columns, literals, or other helpers.


replace_when()
replace_when(mixed $x, array ...$cases): Vec
Like case_when(), but rows matching no case keep x’s value: replace_when('score', [fn ($r) => $r->score > 8, 8]).
Returns a vector helper (Vec). Its expression runs on a database table when its arguments are columns, literals, or other helpers. Example.


recode()
recode(mixed $_x, mixed ...$replacements): Vec
Replace values by name (superseded in dplyr by recode_values()): recode('grade', a: 'A', b: 'B', _default: 'other'), or with a map for keys that aren’t valid names: recode('code', [1 => 'one', 2 => 'two']). The first argument is dplyr’s .x. Values match by their string form. Unmatched values stay as they are unless _default is given; NA becomes _missing.
Returns a vector helper (Vec). Its expression runs on a database table when its arguments are columns, literals, or other helpers. An unknown underscored option throws InvalidArgumentException.


recode_values()
recode_values(mixed $x, mixed ...$cases): Vec
Map values to new values (dplyr 1.2): recode_values('state', ['NC', 'North Carolina'], [['NY', 'NYC'], 'New York'], default: 'other'), or with a lookup table: recode_values('score', from: [1, 2, 3], to: ['low', 'mid', 'high']). Unmatched values get default (NA by default); unmatched: ‘error’ throws instead.
Returns a vector helper (Vec). Its expression runs on a database table when its arguments are columns, literals, or other helpers. Example.


replace_values()
replace_values(mixed $x, mixed ...$cases): Vec
Like recode_values(), but unmatched values keep their original value.
Returns a vector helper (Vec). Its expression runs on a database table when its arguments are columns, literals, or other helpers.


coalesce()
coalesce(mixed $x, mixed ...$values): Vec
First non-NA value across the arguments, row by row.
Returns a vector helper (Vec). Its expression runs on a database table when its arguments are columns, literals, or other helpers. Example.


na_if()
na_if(mixed $x, mixed $y): Vec
NA where $x equals $y.
Returns a vector helper (Vec). Its expression runs on a database table when its arguments are columns, literals, or other helpers.


between()
between(mixed $x, mixed $left, mixed $right): Vec
$left <= $x <= $right; NA when $x is NA.
Returns a vector helper (Vec). Its expression runs on a database table when its arguments are columns, literals, or other helpers.


near()
near(mixed $x, mixed $y, ?float $tol = null): Vec
Equality with tolerance, for floating point.
Returns a vector helper (Vec). Its expression runs on a database table when its arguments are columns, literals, or other helpers.


when_any()
when_any(mixed ...$conditions): Vec
Elementwise any() across conditions (x | y | z): when_any(fn ($r) => ..., 'flag'). With naRm, NA inputs are ignored.
Returns a vector helper (Vec). Its expression runs on a database table when its arguments are columns, literals, or other helpers. Example.


when_all()
when_all(mixed ...$conditions): Vec
Elementwise all() across conditions (x & y & z).
Returns a vector helper (Vec). Its expression runs on a database table when its arguments are columns, literals, or other helpers.

title: tidyselect and across()
text:
Selectors pick columns by name, pattern, or type. They work in select(), relocate(), rename_with(), arrange(), distinct(), group_by(), count(), across(), pick(), and the tidyr functions.







Selector
Columns




'x', ['x', 'y']
By name


starts_with('x'), ends_with(), contains()
By name fragment; case-insensitive unless ignoreCase: false


matches('^x\\d+$')
By regular expression


num_range('x', 1, 3)
x1, x2, x3


everything(), last_col()
All columns, the last column


all_of([...]), any_of([...])
Names from a list, strict or lenient


where('numeric'), where(fn ($values, $type, $name) => ...)
By type or predicate


group_cols()
The grouping columns


except(...)
Everything but these (dplyr’s -x)


any_selected(...), all_selected(...)
Union and intersection



where() accepts 'numeric', 'integer', 'double', 'character', 'logical', 'factor', 'date', 'datetime', 'time', and 'list', or a Phibble\Type. 'numeric' selects integer and double columns. 'time' selects phibble’s time columns, R’s hms, and needs phibble 0.6 or later.


starts_with(array|string $prefix, bool $ignoreCase = true): Selector
Columns whose names start with a prefix (case-insensitive by default).
Returns Selector. Pivot between wide and long.



ends_with(array|string $suffix, bool $ignoreCase = true): Selector
Columns whose names end with a suffix (case-insensitive by default).
Returns Selector. Example.



contains(array|string $needle, bool $ignoreCase = true): Selector
Columns whose names contain a string (case-insensitive by default).
Returns Selector.



matches(string $pattern, bool $ignoreCase = true): Selector
Columns whose names match a regular expression. Bare patterns are wrapped in delimiters; case-insensitive by default.
Returns Selector.



num_range(string $prefix, int $from, int $to, int $width = 0): Selector
Columns named prefix + number for each number: num_range('x', 1, 3).
Returns Selector.



everything(): Selector
Every column.
Returns Selector.



last_col(int $offset = 0): Selector
The last column, or the one $offset before it.
Returns Selector. Throws OutOfRangeException on invalid arguments.



all_of(array $names): Selector
Exactly these columns; all must exist.
Returns Selector.



any_of(array $names): Selector
These columns, skipping any that don’t exist.
Returns Selector.



where(Closure|Phibble\Type|string $predicate): Selector
Columns for which a predicate holds. The predicate receives (list $values, Type $type, string $name). Shortcuts: a Phibble, or one of ‘numeric’, ‘integer’, ‘double’, ‘character’, ‘logical’, ‘factor’, ‘date’, ‘datetime’, ‘time’ (phibble 0.6 and later), ‘list’.
Returns Selector. Throws InvalidArgumentException on invalid arguments.



except(mixed ...$columns): Selector
Everything except these columns: select(except('id')) is dplyr’s select(-id).
Returns Selector.



any_selected(mixed ...$selections): Selector
Columns matched by any of the selections (union).
Returns Selector.



all_selected(mixed ...$selections): Selector
Columns matched by every selection (intersection, like a & b in tidyselect).
Returns Selector.



group_cols(): Selector
The grouping columns.
Returns Selector.

title: tidyselect and across()
text:
across()
across(cols, fns, names:) applies functions to several columns inside mutate() or summarize(). Grouping columns are never selected. fns is one function or an associative array of named functions. Output names default to {col} for one function and {col}_{fn} for several.

PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


$penguins = DataFrame::fromCsv("$data/penguins.csv") |>
    drop_na() |>
    group_by('species');

// Phplyr helpers can be passed by name; each gets the column name.
echo $penguins |>
    summarize(across(ends_with('_mm'), ['avg' => mean(...), 'sd' => sd(...)]));

// Other closures get the column's values (summarize) or each value (mutate).
echo "\n", $penguins |>
    summarize(across(['flipper_length_mm', 'body_mass_g'], fn (array $v) => \max($v) - \min($v), names: 'range_{col}'));
echo "\n", $penguins |> ungroup() |> mutate(across(ends_with('_mm'), fn ($v) => round($v))) |> head(3);


$penguins = phplyr(DataFrame::fromCsv("$data/penguins.csv"))
    ->dropNa()
    ->groupBy('species')
    ->get();

// Phplyr helpers can be passed by name; each gets the column name.
echo phplyr($penguins)

title: Models
text:
lm(), glm(), lmer(), and glmer() fit models with phit. phit reads factor levels from the table, builds the model matrix from an R formula, and fits the model. phplyr adds no model code of its own.
With phit 0.3, which predates these names, phplyr calls phit 0.3’s fit_lm(), fit_glm(), fit_lmer(), and fit_glmer().
The functions come from the phit extension or from phit-polyfill, its PHP port, and phplyr calls both the same way. phit’s Extension or polyfill page compares them. The Models benchmark times both through phplyr.
CI runs phplyr’s tests with each implementation. Both runs compare lm() and glm() coefficients with R’s, and lmer() fixed effects with lme4’s. The Models verification lists the comparisons.

title: Databases and expressions
Porting an R script
text:
A typical R analysis of the penguins data, translated to PHP. It reads a CSV file, cleans and reshapes it, summarizes it, and fits a linear, a logistic, and a random-intercept model.
Data: penguins, size measurements for 344 penguins near Palmer Station, Antarctica, read by URL. The R script needs dplyr, tidyr, and lme4. The PHP script needs phplyr and, for the models, phit; see Models.

title: Porting an R script
text:
What changed in translation

Loading. read.csv() becomes DataFrame::fromCsv(), which infers column types like readr and reads empty fields as NA, as na.strings = c("", "NA") does in R.
Pipes. On PHP 8.5, R’s |> stays |>. On PHP 8.3 and 8.4, the pipeline becomes a method chain that starts with phplyr($t).
Column references. Bare names become strings, or col('x') inside expressions, so bill_length_mm / bill_depth_mm becomes col('bill_length_mm')->div(col('bill_depth_mm')).
Conditions. case_when(x < 4 ~ "low", .default = "high") becomes case_when([col('x')->lt(4), 'low'], default: 'high').
Renaming in select. select(length = bill_length_mm) becomes select(['length' => 'bill_length_mm']).
Column sets. c(length, depth) becomes ['length', 'depth'].
Models. lm(), glm(), and lmer() take the same formulas. They return arrays, so coef() and fixef() become reads of coefficients. The coefficients agree to the printed four decimals, except the last digit of the random-intercept model’s intercept.
Printing. DataFrames print in tibble’s format.

On a database table from Phibble\tbl(), the cleaning, counting, and grouped-summary steps run as SQL, because they use col() expressions and phplyr’s helpers. The reshaping step loads the rows into PHP. See Databases and expressions.

title: phplyr

phplyr
text:
phplyr and phibble
The tables come from phibble, which Composer installs with phplyr. phplyr adds dplyr’s and tidyr’s functions on top of phibble’s table methods, so a pipeline runs on an in-memory DataFrame, on a database table as SQL, or on Polars.

dplyr’s single-table and two-table functions, with grouped window functions, across(), column selectors, and join_by() conditions.

title: Compatibility and limitations
text:
Backends
A phplyr function calls the methods of phibble’s Table contract, so a pipeline runs on any table that implements it:

Phibble\DataFrame holds the data in PHP memory.
Phibble\tbl($pdo, 'table') builds SQL for SQLite, PostgreSQL, or MySQL. A function given a PHP closure, and an expression without a SQL translation, runs the query so far, loads the rows, and continues in memory. Databases and expressions lists those expressions.
Phibble\Polars\PolarsTable belongs to phibble and runs pipelines in Polars through the phpolars extension. A closure step converts the data to a DataFrame and back.

title: Compatibility and limitations
text:
Not supported

Bare column names and tidy evaluation. Columns are strings, and expressions are closures, helpers, or col() expressions.
mutate(_keep: 'used') and _keep: 'unused' with closures. These work with expression arguments such as col('x')->mul(2), whose columns phplyr can read. A PHP closure does not expose the columns it reads, so phplyr throws an InvalidArgumentException.
cur_data() and cur_data_all(), which dplyr has deprecated. Use pick().
Data frame columns and across(.unpack). pack() makes a column of named arrays.
The scoped _at, _if, and _all variants, such as mutate_at(). Use across().
janitor’s adorn_*() functions and three-way tabyl().

title: Compatibility and limitations
text:
Differences in behavior

_by sorts groups. dplyr keeps the order of first appearance for .by. phplyr sorts by key, as it does for group_by().
Strings are UTF-8. String functions count UTF-8 characters.
Date-times parse to UTC unless a function is given tz:, whatever PHP’s default time zone is, as in lubridate.
Models return arrays. lm() and the other model functions return phit’s result array, with R’s coefficient names in columns, in place of a model object.

Conventions

Positions are 1-based, as in R: pull(1) is the first column, pull(-1) the last, and slice(1, 3) the first and third rows of each group.
var() is var_(), because var is a reserved word in PHP. variance() is an alias.
summarise() and summarize() are the same function, as in dplyr.
count(), min(), max(), rename(), and other functions have the names of PHP built-ins. In a file that imports them, write \count() for the built-in. Imports lists them.
Group order follows dplyr: groups are sorted by key, factors by level order, and NA last. _by also sorts groups (dplyr keeps first-appearance order for .by).

title: Coming from dplyr
text:
phplyr options and phibble methods
phplyr functions and phibble methods both take and return phibble tables, so a pipeline can use both. phibble’s methods have their own conventions:

A phibble method takes an array: $df->mutate(['z' => $expr]), $df->groupBy(['g']), $df->arrange([['x', 'desc']]). A phplyr function takes named arguments: mutate(z: ...), group_by('g'), arrange(desc('x')).
phibble methods have no underscored options. Grouping is a separate method call, and summarise(array $aggregates, ?string $groups) takes the .groups value as a second argument.
A phplyr helper such as mean('x') builds a phibble expression, which a database table can compile to SQL. See Databases and expressions.

title: Coming from dplyr
text:
across() functions
R passes a vector to every across() function. In phplyr, what a function receives depends on the function and on the table function that calls it. See across().

The tests use Pest and run under PHP 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5. They call functions through pipe(), so they parse on every version. tests/Pipe/ holds the tests written with |>; bin/test leaves them out before PHP 8.5.

text:
Documentation
The site is a Quarto project in docs/. Code examples live in docs/examples/*.php. bin/docs-examples runs each one with docs/ as the working directory and writes docs/examples/_<name>.md with the code and its output, which the pages include. Rendering never executes PHP.
An example uses |>, and docs/examples/<name>.chain.php beside it is the same example as a method chain. bin/docs-examples runs both and fails if their output differs. The page shows the two in tabs labeled “PHP 8.5+” and “PHP 8.3–8.4”, with the output once. bin/docs-examples needs PHP 8.5, and it loads phit from .ext/libphit.dylib for the model examples.
Most examples leave out the require line and the imports, and bin/docs-examples adds them before it runs the code, with $data set to the PHPstats datasets folder. Examples read their data from there by URL, so they need network access. An example that requires vendor/autoload.php itself is a complete script. It runs as written, so a missing import fails the run, and the page shows it without the opening tag and the require line. The first example, the porting script, and the pages in the Examples section (docs/examples/<slug>.qmd, with their code in docs/examples/pages/) are complete scripts. A subdirectory’s _prelude.php, such as the Gallery’s, replaces the generated prelude for its examples, and the page shows it once.
PHP=/path/to/php85 bin/docs-examples   # refresh example output
PHP=/path/to/php85 bin/render-docs     # examples, quarto render, publish to docs/
The first example reads penguins by URL from the datasets repository’s main branch, and a test checks that the README and site.json do the same.

phplyr’s functions are namespaced functions in Phplyr. Import the ones a file uses with use function. The snippets in the reference pages leave the imports out.
use Phibble\DataFrame;

Some phplyr functions have the same names as PHP built-in functions. In a file that imports one of them, the bare name calls phplyr’s function. Write a leading backslash to call the built-in, as in \count($array).

text:
Pipelines
A table function such as filter(...) returns a closure that takes a table and returns a new one. A pipeline applies such closures in order.

PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


The pipe operator |> calls the closure on its right with the value on its left:
$out = $penguins |>
    filter(fn ($r) => $r->body_mass_g > 5000) |>
    arrange(desc('body_mass_g'));


phplyr($table) starts a method chain. Each method calls the phplyr function of the same name with the same arguments. A chained method is camelCase, so group_by() is ->groupBy() and n_groups() is ->nGroups(). get() returns the table:
$out = phplyr($penguins)
    ->filter(fn ($r) => $r->body_mass_g > 5000)
    ->arrange(desc('body_mass_g'))
    ->get();



The two forms give the same result, and the documentation shows both.
A method chain stays a chain while each method returns a table. These functions return something else, and the chain returns that value:

phit’s result array



echo prints a chain’s table without get(). ->pipe($closure) applies a closure of your own and continues the chain with its result.
pipe() applies closures in order on every PHP version:
$out = pipe($penguins, filter(fn ($r) => $r->body_mass_g > 5000), arrange(desc('body_mass_g')));

section: Columns, row closures, and vector helpers

title: Getting started
text:
Named arguments and options
Functions that create columns name them with PHP named arguments: mutate(total: ...), summarize(n: n()). An option that dplyr writes with a leading dot, such as .by, is written with a leading underscore, such as _by:. Any other named argument is a column, so mutate(_before: 'id') places the new columns and mutate(before: 1) makes a column called before. Underscored arguments lists them.
PHP does not allow positional arguments after named ones. Put across() and other positional arguments first: summarize(across(...), n: n()).

title: Getting started
text:
Printing and inspecting
echo prints a table. glimpse() prints one line per column and returns the table unchanged, so it can sit inside a pipeline. pull('x') returns a column as a PHP array, and $table->toRows() returns every row as an array.

title: Performance
text: phplyr’s functions call one or two methods of the table they are given, so the backend determines how fast a pipeline runs. Benchmarks has the timings of phibble’s workloads and of three pipelines on each backend and in dplyr.

title: Performance
text:
Choosing a backend

In-memory DataFrame suits data that fits in memory. Expression arguments, such as mean('x') and col('x')->gt(0), run faster than closures, because phibble computes expressions in one pass without building a table per group.
A database table (Phibble\tbl()) avoids loading the data into PHP. With expressions, filter() and summarise() run in the database, and only the result reaches PHP.
Pipelines that return every row (mutate(), arrange(), unfiltered joins) spend most of their database time transferring rows to PHP.
Closures on a database table load all rows first and then run in memory. Use col() expressions and phplyr’s helpers to keep the work in SQL.
SQLite columns need declared types. PDO binds values as strings. In an untyped column, SQLite stores them as text and compares numbers as text.
PolarsTable (phibble’s Polars backend, on the phpolars extension) runs expressions in Polars and converts the result to PHP values. Workloads that reduce the data gain the most. Workloads that return every row after little computation, such as a mutate() or a join, spend most of their time converting the result.
Closure steps on PolarsTable convert the data to a DataFrame and back, so closures run slower on PolarsTable than on DataFrame.
Data that starts in Polars can skip phibble’s CSV parse with PolarsTable::fromPolars(Phpolars\read_csv($path)).

title: Pipes and method chains
text: A table function such as filter(...) returns a closure that takes a table. The PHP 8.5 pipe operator |>, pipe(), and a method chain started with phplyr() apply such closures in order and give the same result. Pipelines shows the three forms.

title: Pipes and method chains
text:
Pipelines

phplyr()
phplyr(Table|Chain $table): Chain
Start a method chain on a table: phplyr($t)->filter(...)->head(5). Each method runs the phplyr function of that name, spelled camelCase, so ->groupBy() runs group_by(). get() returns the table, and functions that return something else, such as pull(), return it plainly.
Returns Chain.


pipe()
pipe(mixed $value, callable ...$steps): mixed
Apply steps to a value in order: pipe($t, filter(...), head(5)) is $t |> filter(...) |> head(5). A step is any callable.
Returns mixed.

title: Pipes and method chains
text:
Chain methods
phplyr($table) returns a Phplyr\Chain. Each table function runs as the chain method of the same name in camelCase, such as ->groupBy() for group_by(); Functions and methods lists them. A method whose function returns a table returns a new chain, and any other result is returned as it is. A snake_case method name throws BadMethodCallException naming the camelCase method.

->get()
$chain->get(): Table
Returns the chain’s table.


->pipe()
$chain->pipe(callable ...$steps): mixed
Applies each step to the table in order. Returns a new chain when the result is a table, and the result itself otherwise.


echo
echo $chain;
Prints the table, as echo $table does.

text:
Row-wise operations
rowwise() makes each row its own group. Closures in summarize() and vector helpers then see one row at a time. Optional id columns stay as groups in the result of summarize(). c_across(cols) gives the current row’s values of the selected columns, for helpers such as sum(c_across(starts_with('x'))).

PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


echo DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['id' => 'a', 'q1' => 3, 'q2' => 5, 'q3' => null],
    ['id' => 'b', 'q1' => 4, 'q2' => 1, 'q3' => 2],
]) |>
    rowwise('id') |>
    summarize(total: fn ($row) => Stats::sum(
        [...$row->column('q1'), ...$row->column('q2'), ...$row->column('q3')],
        naRm: true,
    ));


echo phplyr(DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['id' => 'a', 'q1' => 3, 'q2' => 5, 'q3' => null],
    ['id' => 'b', 'q1' => 4, 'q2' => 1, 'q3' => 2],
]))
    ->rowwise('id')
    ->summarize(total: fn ($row) => Stats::sum(
        [...$row->column('q1'), ...$row->column('q2'), ...$row->column('q3')],
        naRm: true,

title: janitor
text: phplyr has the single-table functions from R’s janitor package, with janitor 2.2’s rules.

title: janitor
text:
Clean names
clean_names() renames every column of a table, and make_clean_names() applies the same rules to a list of strings. The rules follow janitor’s defaults:

% becomes percent, # becomes number, and quotes are dropped.
Accented and non-Latin characters are transliterated to ASCII: Café becomes cafe, straße becomes strasse, and αβγ becomes abg.
Spaces and punctuation become single underscores, and leading and trailing ones are dropped.
Case changes split words: camelCaseVar becomes camel_case_var, and HTMLParser becomes html_parser. Digits stay attached to their word.
A name that would start with a digit gets an x prefix, and an empty name becomes x.
A repeated name gets _2, _3, and so on, in order of appearance.

Transliteration uses ext-intl, which gives the same results as janitor’s stringi. Without ext-intl, phplyr falls back to iconv, and some names can differ from janitor’s.
make_clean_names(['First Name', 'first_name', '% Done', '1st Place']);
// ['first_name', 'first_name_2', 'percent_done', 'x1st_place']

pipe($survey, clean_names());

make_clean_names()
make_clean_names(array $names): array
janitor’s make_clean_names(): snake_case names that are unique, ASCII, and start with a letter. ‘%’ becomes “percent”, ‘#’ becomes “number”, accents and other scripts are transliterated (with ext-intl, as janitor does with stringi), names that would start with a digit get an “x” prefix, and repeats get _2, _3, … suffixes.
Returns array.


clean_names()
clean_names(): Closure
Rename every column with make_clean_names(), as janitor’s clean_names().
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->cleanNames().

title: janitor
text:
Remove empty rows and columns
remove_empty() drops rows and columns that are entirely NA. Pass 'rows' or 'cols' to drop only one kind. With cutoff below 1, a row or column is kept when its share of non-NA values is above the cutoff. A cutoff works with only one of 'rows' and 'cols'. An empty string is a value, as in R.

remove_empty()
remove_empty(array|string $which = ['rows', 'cols'], float $cutoff = 1.0): Closure
Drop rows and/or columns that are entirely NA, as janitor’s remove_empty(). With a cutoff below 1 (for rows or cols alone), keep those whose share of non-NA values is above the cutoff.
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->removeEmpty(). Throws InvalidArgumentException on invalid arguments.

title: janitor
text:
Duplicates
get_dupes('email') returns the rows whose values in the given columns appear more than once. The result has the given columns first, then dupe_count, then the other columns. Rows are sorted by dupe_count (descending) and then by the given columns. With no columns, every column is used. A grouped table keeps its groups, but duplicates are found across the whole table.

get_dupes()
get_dupes(mixed ...$columns): Closure
Rows whose values in these columns (all columns when none are given) appear more than once, as janitor’s get_dupes(): the columns, then dupe_count, then the rest, sorted by dupe_count (descending) and the columns. Grouping is kept but not used.
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->getDupes().

title: janitor
text:
Frequency tables
tabyl('g') counts the values of one column. The result has the values, n, and percent. When the column has NAs, valid_percent gives each share with NA left out. showNa: false drops the NA row instead.
tabyl('g', 'h') counts pairs of values. It has one row per value of g and one column of counts per value of h. An NA in h is counted in the NA_ column, and an empty string in the emptystring_ column.
Values are sorted as in dplyr’s count(), with NA last. Factors keep their level order, and showMissingLevels: false leaves out unused levels.
pipe($people, tabyl('region'));
pipe($people, tabyl('region', 'smoker', showNa: false));
janitor’s adorn_*() functions and three-way tables are not included.

tabyl()
tabyl(string $var1, ?string $var2 = null, bool $showNa = true, bool $showMissingLevels = true): Closure
janitor’s tabyl() for one or two columns. One column gives its values with n and percent (and valid_percent, which leaves NA out, when there are NAs). Two columns give a crosstab of counts: one row per value of the first, one column per value of the second (“NA_” for NA, “emptystring_” for ““). Values sort as dplyr’s count() does, with NA last and factors in level order.
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->tabyl().

title: Single-table functions
text:
filter() keeps rows where every condition is true. Conditions are row closures, vector helpers such as between() or if_any(), or the name of a logical column. NA counts as false. filter_out() drops the rows where every condition is true and keeps rows where a condition is NA, so filter() and filter_out() with the same conditions split a table without overlap.

PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


$penguins = DataFrame::fromCsv("$data/penguins.csv");

// Several conditions are combined with AND; NA counts as false.
echo $penguins |>
    filter(fn ($r) => $r->bill_length_mm > 50, between('flipper_length_mm', 190, 200)) |>
    select('species', 'island', 'bill_length_mm', 'flipper_length_mm');

// filter_out() drops the rows where every condition is true.
echo "\n", $penguins |> filter_out(fn ($r) => $r->species === 'Adelie') |> count();


$penguins = DataFrame::fromCsv("$data/penguins.csv");

// Several conditions are combined with AND; NA counts as false.
echo phplyr($penguins)
    ->filter(fn ($r) => $r->bill_length_mm > 50, between('flipper_length_mm', 190, 200))
    ->select('species', 'island', 'bill_length_mm', 'flipper_length_mm');

echo "\n", phplyr($penguins)->filterOut(fn ($r) => $r->species === 'Adelie')->count();

filter() keeps rows where every condition is true. Conditions are row closures, vector helpers such as between() or if_any(), or the name of a logical column. NA counts as false. filter_out() drops the rows where every condition is true and keeps rows where a condition is NA, so filter() and filter_out() with the same conditions split a table without overlap.

$penguins = DataFrame::fromCsv("$data/penguins.csv");

echo $penguins |>

    select('species', 'island', 'bill_length_mm', 'flipper_length_mm');

// filter_out() drops the rows where every condition is true.
echo "\n", $penguins |> filter_out(fn ($r) => $r->species === 'Adelie') |> count();


$penguins = DataFrame::fromCsv("$data/penguins.csv");

// Several conditions are combined with AND; NA counts as false.
echo phplyr($penguins)
    ->filter(fn ($r) => $r->bill_length_mm > 50, between('flipper_length_mm', 190, 200))
    ->select('species', 'island', 'bill_length_mm', 'flipper_length_mm');

// filter_out() drops the rows where every condition is true.
echo "\n", phplyr($penguins)->filterOut(fn ($r) => $r->species === 'Adelie')->count();

Single-table functions
text:
Summaries
summarize() returns one row per group. summarise() is the same function. Each named argument is a summary helper or a closure that receives the group’s table and returns one value. With several grouping columns, the result drops the last one, as in dplyr. _groups accepts 'drop_last', 'drop', 'keep', and 'rowwise'.

PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


echo DataFrame::fromCsv("$data/penguins.csv") |>
    summarize(
        penguins: n(),
        species: n_distinct('species'),
        median_mass_g: median('body_mass_g', naRm: true),
        q90_flipper_mm: quantile('flipper_length_mm', 0.9, naRm: true),
        iqr_bill_mm: iqr('bill_length_mm', naRm: true),
        heaviest: fn ($g) => ($g |> slice_max('body_mass_g', n: 1) |> pull('species'))[0],
    );


echo phplyr(DataFrame::fromCsv("$data/penguins.csv"))
    ->summarize(
        penguins: n(),
        species: n_distinct('species'),
        median_mass_g: median('body_mass_g', naRm: true),
        q90_flipper_mm: quantile('flipper_length_mm', 0.9, naRm: true),
        iqr_bill_mm: iqr('bill_length_mm', naRm: true),
        heaviest: fn ($g) => phplyr($g)->sliceMax('body_mass_g', n: 1)->pull('species')[0],
    );

    ->dropNa('body_mass_g')

text: The tidyr functions use tidyr’s argument names in camelCase, and tidyr’s dot-arguments take a leading underscore. See Underscored arguments.

title: tidyr
text:
Pivoting
pivot_longer(cols) turns the selected columns into rows of names and values.








Option
Default
Effect




namesTo
'name'
Column, or columns, for the names. '.value' takes a value column’s name from that part.


valuesTo
'value'
Column for the values


namesPrefix
none
Regular expression removed from the start of each name


namesSep, namesPattern
none
Split names into several namesTo columns, by separator or by regex groups


valuesDropNa
false
Drop rows whose values are all NA


namesTransform, valuesTransform
none
A closure, or an array of closures by column


colsVary
'fastest'
'slowest' keeps each source column’s rows together



pivot_wider() spreads names and values into columns.








Option
Default
Effect




namesFrom, valuesFrom
'name', 'value'
Columns that supply the new names and their values


idCols
every other column
Columns that identify the output rows


valuesFill
NA
Value for missing cells


valuesFn
none
Combines duplicate cells


namesPrefix, namesSep, namesGlue, namesSort
'', '_', none, false
Control the new names


namesVary
'fastest'
'slowest' groups each name’s value columns together


namesExpand, idExpand
false
Add every combination of the namesFrom or idCols values, sorted, factors by level


unusedFn
none
Summarizes columns in none of idCols, namesFrom, and valuesFrom



Without valuesFn, duplicate cells turn the value columns into list-columns and trigger a PHP warning with tidyr’s message.
build_longer_spec() and build_wider_spec() return tidyr’s pivot spec as a table, and pivot_longer_spec() and pivot_wider_spec() run an edited one. The superseded gather() and spread() are also available.

PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


$scores = DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['student' => 'ann', 'wk1' => 10, 'wk2' => null, 'wk3' => 30],
    ['student' => 'bob', 'wk1' => 7, 'wk2' => 8, 'wk3' => 9],
]);

$long = $scores |> pivot_longer(starts_with('wk'), namesTo: 'week', namesPrefix: 'wk', valuesTo: 'points', valuesDropNa: true);
echo $long;

echo "\n", $long |> pivot_wider(namesFrom: 'week', valuesFrom: 'points', namesPrefix: 'week_', valuesFill: 0, namesSort: true);


$scores = DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['student' => 'ann', 'wk1' => 10, 'wk2' => null, 'wk3' => 30],
    ['student' => 'bob', 'wk1' => 7, 'wk2' => 8, 'wk3' => 9],
]);

$long = phplyr($scores)->pivotLonger(starts_with('wk'), namesTo: 'week', namesPrefix: 'wk', valuesTo: 'points', valuesDropNa: true)->get();
echo $long;

echo "\n", phplyr($long)->pivotWider(namesFrom: 'week', valuesFrom: 'points', namesPrefix: 'week_', valuesFill: 0, namesSort: true);

pivot_longer(mixed $cols, array|string $namesTo = 'name', string $valuesTo = 'value', ?string $namesPrefix = null, ?string $namesSep = null, ?string $namesPattern = null, bool $valuesDropNa = false, Closure|array|null $namesTransform = null, Closure|array|null $valuesTransform = null, string $colsVary = 'fastest'): Closure

text:
Missing combinations and values
complete() adds missing combinations of the given columns and fills other columns with NA, or with values from fill:. A column name expands to its unique values (a factor to its levels), nesting() keeps only combinations that occur, and a named list supplies the values. It works within groups. expand() returns only the combinations, and crossing() and expand_grid() build a new table from lists.

PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


echo DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['shop' => 'north', 'month' => 1, 'sales' => 10],
    ['shop' => 'north', 'month' => 3, 'sales' => 12],
    ['shop' => 'south', 'month' => 2, 'sales' => 7],
]) |>
    complete('shop', month: [1, 2, 3], fill: ['sales' => 0]);


echo phplyr(DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['shop' => 'north', 'month' => 1, 'sales' => 10],
    ['shop' => 'north', 'month' => 3, 'sales' => 12],
    ['shop' => 'south', 'month' => 2, 'sales' => 7],
]))
    ->complete('shop', month: [1, 2, 3], fill: ['sales' => 0]);



# A tibble: 6 × 3
  shop  month sales
  <chr> <int> <int>
1 north     1    10
2 north     2     0
3 north     3    12
4 south     1     0
5 south     2     7
6 south     3     0
fill() carries values down or up over NA within groups (_direction: 'down' | 'up' | 'downup' | 'updown'). drop_na() drops rows with NA in the given columns, and replace_na() replaces NA per column.

PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


echo DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['quarter' => 'Q1', 'year' => 2024, 'sales' => 10],
    ['quarter' => 'Q2', 'year' => null, 'sales' => null],
    ['quarter' => 'Q3', 'year' => null, 'sales' => 14],
]) |>
    fill('year') |>
    replace_na(['sales' => 0]);


echo phplyr(DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['quarter' => 'Q1', 'year' => 2024, 'sales' => 10],
    ['quarter' => 'Q2', 'year' => null, 'sales' => null],
    ['quarter' => 'Q3', 'year' => null, 'sales' => 14],
]))
    ->fill('year')
    ->replaceNa(['sales' => 0]);



# A tibble: 3 × 3
  quarter  year sales
  <chr>   <int> <int>
1 Q1       2024    10
2 Q2       2024     0
3 Q3       2024    14

complete()
complete(mixed ...$items): Closure
Add missing combinations, filling other columns with NA (or with fill). complete('year', 'type', fill: ['n' => 0]). Option: explicit (default true; false fills only the added rows).
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->complete(). Example.


expand()
expand(mixed ...$items): Closure
Every combination of the given columns, per group: expand('year', 'type'), expand(nesting('id', 'name'), 'year'), expand(year: range(2000, 2005)).
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->expand().


nesting()
nesting(mixed ...$columns): Nesting
Only the combinations that occur in the data, for complete() and expand().
Returns Nesting.


crossing()
crossing(array ...$columns): Phibble\DataFrame
Every combination of unique values (sorted), as a new table: crossing(x: [1, 2], y: ['a', 'b']).
Returns Phibble\DataFrame.


expand_grid()
expand_grid(array ...$columns): Phibble\DataFrame
Every combination of the values as given, first column varying slowest.
Returns Phibble\DataFrame.


full_seq()
full_seq(array $x, int|float $period, float $tol = 1.0E-6): array
Every value from the smallest to the largest of x in steps of period: full_seq([1, 5, 3], 1) is [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Values off the grid (beyond tol) are an error.
Returns array. Throws InvalidArgumentException on invalid arguments.


fill()
fill(mixed ...$cols): Closure
Fill NA with the previous (or next) value, within groups: fill('price', _direction: 'down'|'up'|'downup'|'updown').
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->fill(). Throws InvalidArgumentException on invalid arguments. An unknown underscored option throws InvalidArgumentException. Example.


drop_na()
drop_na(mixed ...$cols): Closure
Drop rows with NA in any of the columns (any column when none are given).
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->dropNa().


replace_na()
replace_na(array $replace): Closure
Replace NA per column: replace_na(['n' => 0, 'label' => 'unknown']).
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->replaceNa(). Example.


uncount()
uncount(mixed $weights, bool $_remove = true, ?string $_id = null): Closure
Repeat each row by a weight column: uncount('n'). Options: _remove (drop the weight column, default true), _id (add a 1-based copy number).
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->uncount(). Throws InvalidArgumentException on invalid arguments.

Splitting and combining







Function
Use




separate_wider_delim(col, delim, names:)
Split on a fixed string into columns

Split with named regular expressions

List-columns of tables

Every value from the smallest to the largest in steps of period



tooFew and tooMany handle pieces that don’t fit, as in tidyr.

PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


$t = DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['id' => 1, 'name' => 'Ada Lovelace', 'tags' => 'math,code'],
    ['id' => 2, 'name' => 'Grace Hopper', 'tags' => 'navy'],

echo $t |> separate_wider_delim('name', ' ', names: ['first', 'last']);
echo "\n", $t |> select('id', 'tags') |> separate_longer_delim('tags', ',');
echo "\n", $t |> select('id', 'name') |> unite('label', 'id', 'name', sep: ': ');


$t = DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['id' => 1, 'name' => 'Ada Lovelace', 'tags' => 'math,code'],
    ['id' => 2, 'name' => 'Grace Hopper', 'tags' => 'navy'],
]);

echo phplyr($t)->separateWiderDelim('name', ' ', names: ['first', 'last']);
echo "\n", phplyr($t)->select('id', 'tags')->separateLongerDelim('tags', ',');
echo "\n", phplyr($t)->select('id', 'name')->unite('label', 'id', 'name', sep: ': ');

2     2 Grace Hopper   navy

1     1 math 
2     1 code 
3     2 navy

separate_wider_delim()
separate_wider_delim(mixed $cols, string $delim, ?array $names = null, ?string $namesSep = null, string $tooFew = 'error', string $tooMany = 'error', bool $colsRemove = true): Closure
Split columns on a fixed delimiter into new columns: separate_wider_delim('name', ' ', names: ['first', 'last']). Without names, give namesSep to name them col{sep}1, col{sep}2… tooFew: ‘error’|‘align_start’|‘align_end’; tooMany: ‘error’|‘drop’|‘merge’.
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->separateWiderDelim(). Throws InvalidArgumentException, UnexpectedValueException on invalid arguments. Example.


separate_wider_position()
separate_wider_position(mixed $cols, array $widths, string $tooFew = 'error', bool $colsRemove = true): Closure
Split columns by character widths: separate_wider_position('code', ['state' => 2, 1, 'county' => 3]); unnamed widths are skipped.
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->separateWiderPosition(). Throws UnexpectedValueException on invalid arguments.


separate_wider_regex()
separate_wider_regex(mixed $cols, array $patterns, string $tooFew = 'error', bool $colsRemove = true): Closure
Split columns with regular expressions: separate_wider_regex('id', ['letters' => '[a-z]+', '-', 'digits' => '\d+']). Unnamed patterns match but are not kept. Rows that don’t match error unless tooFew: ‘align_start’.
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->separateWiderRegex(). Throws UnexpectedValueException on invalid arguments.


separate_longer_delim()
separate_longer_delim(mixed $cols, string $delim): Closure
Split columns on a fixed delimiter into rows: separate_longer_delim('tags', ','). Several columns must split into the same number of pieces (or one).
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->separateLongerDelim(). Example.


separate_longer_position()
separate_longer_position(mixed $cols, int $width): Closure
Split columns into rows of $width characters.
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->separateLongerPosition().


separate()
separate(string $col, array $into, array|string|int $sep = '[^[:alnum:]]+', bool $remove = true, bool $convert = false, string $extra = 'warn', string $fill = 'warn'): Closure
Split a string column into several (superseded in tidyr, still common): separate('date', ['year', 'month'], sep: '-'). sep is a regular expression, or an int / list of ints for positions. extra: ‘warn’|‘drop’|‘merge’; fill: ‘warn’|‘right’|‘left’; convert: R’s type.convert().
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->separate().


separate_rows()
separate_rows(mixed ...$cols): Closure
Split columns on a regular expression into rows (superseded by separate_longer_delim()): separate_rows('tags', sep: ','). Options: sep (default ‘[1.]+’), convert.
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->separateRows().


extract()
extract(string $col, array $into, string $regex = '([[:alnum:]]+)', bool $remove = true, bool $convert = false): Closure
Pull regular-expression groups into new columns (superseded by separate_wider_regex()): extract('x', ['letter', 'digit'], '([a-z])(\d)'). A null name skips a group. Rows that don’t match get NA.
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->extract().


unite()
unite(string $col, mixed ...$cols): Closure
Paste columns together into one: unite('date', 'year', 'month', sep: '-'). Options: sep (’_’), remove (true), naRm (false; NA otherwise prints “NA”).
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->unite(). Example.

List-columns
A list element is a PHP array. A list is R’s unnamed list or vector, and an array with string keys is a named list.

nest()
nest(mixed ...$spec): Closure
Nest columns into a list-column of tables: nest(data: ['x', 'y']), or nest() on a grouped table to nest everything but the groups.
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->nest(). Throws InvalidArgumentException on invalid arguments.


unnest()
unnest(array|string $cols, bool $keepEmpty = false): Closure
Unnest list-columns of tables back into rows.
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->unnest().


unnest_longer()
unnest_longer(mixed $col, ?string $valuesTo = null, ?string $indicesTo = null, ?bool $indicesInclude = null, bool $keepEmpty = false): Closure

title: Joins, binding, and set operations
text:
The join functions take the right-hand table as their first argument. The input table is the left-hand table x.



Function
Rows kept




inner_join($y)
Rows of x with a match in y


left_join($y)
All rows of x


right_join($y)
All rows of y


full_join($y)
All rows of both


semi_join($y)
Rows of x with a match, x’s columns only


anti_join($y)
Rows of x without a match


cross_join($y)
Every combination



by: names the key columns. A string or list joins on columns with the same name in both tables, and an associative array maps differing names: by: ['school' => 'school_id']. The forms mix, as in ['id', 'code' => 'country_code']. Without by:, the tables join on every column they share.

PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


use function Phibble\tribble;

$species = DataFrame::fromCsv("$data/penguins.csv") |>
    group_by('species') |>
    summarize(avg_mass_g: mean('body_mass_g', naRm: true));

// A lookup table with one species that isn't in the data.
$scientific = tribble(
    ['species', 'scientific_name'],
    'Adelie', 'Pygoscelis adeliae',
    'Gentoo', 'Pygoscelis papua',
    'Emperor', 'Aptenodytes forsteri',
);

echo $species |> inner_join($scientific, by: 'species');
echo "\n", $species |> left_join($scientific, by: 'species');
echo "\n", $scientific |> anti_join($species, by: 'species');


use function Phibble\tribble;

$species = phplyr(DataFrame::fromCsv("$data/penguins.csv"))
    ->groupBy('species')
    ->summarize(avg_mass_g: mean('body_mass_g', naRm: true))
    ->get();

// A lookup table with one species that isn't in the data.
$scientific = tribble(
    ['species', 'scientific_name'],
    'Adelie', 'Pygoscelis adeliae',
    'Gentoo', 'Pygoscelis papua',
    'Emperor', 'Aptenodytes forsteri',
);

echo phplyr($species)->innerJoin($scientific, by: 'species');
echo "\n", phplyr($species)->leftJoin($scientific, by: 'species');
echo "\n", phplyr($scientific)->antiJoin($species, by: 'species');

1 Adelie       3701. Pygoscelis adeliae
2 Gentoo       5076. Pygoscelis papua  
# A tibble: 3 × 3

1 Adelie         3701. Pygoscelis adeliae
2 Chinstrap      3733. <NA>

1 Emperor Aptenodytes forsteri
The options follow dplyr 1.1:

suffix: renames clashing non-key columns, ['.x', '.y'] by default.
keep: true keeps y’s key columns.
naMatches: 'never' stops NA keys from matching. By default NA matches NA.
multiple: is 'all', 'any', 'first', or 'last'.
unmatched: 'error' throws when rows would be dropped.
relationship: checks 'one-to-one', 'one-to-many', 'many-to-one', or 'many-to-many', and throws an InvalidArgumentException when the check fails. Without it, an equality join in which keys repeat on both sides triggers an E_USER_WARNING with dplyr’s message and still returns every match. relationship: 'many-to-many' silences it.


PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


$x = DataFrame::fromRows([['id' => 1, 'v' => 'a'], ['id' => 2, 'v' => 'b'], ['id' => null, 'v' => 'c']]);
$y = DataFrame::fromRows([['id' => 2, 'v' => 'B'], ['id' => 2, 'v' => 'B2'], ['id' => null, 'v' => 'C']]);

// Clashing columns get suffixes; NA keys match each other, as in dplyr.
echo $x |> left_join($y, by: 'id');

// Keep only the first match, and never match NA keys.
echo "\n", $x |> left_join($y, by: 'id', multiple: 'first', naMatches: 'never', suffix: ['x', '_y']);


$x = DataFrame::fromRows([['id' => 1, 'v' => 'a'], ['id' => 2, 'v' => 'b'], ['id' => null, 'v' => 'c']]);
$y = DataFrame::fromRows([['id' => 2, 'v' => 'B'], ['id' => 2, 'v' => 'B2'], ['id' => null, 'v' => 'C']]);

// Clashing columns get suffixes; NA keys match each other, as in dplyr.
echo phplyr($x)->leftJoin($y, by: 'id');

// Keep only the first match, and never match NA keys.
echo "\n", phplyr($x)->leftJoin($y, by: 'id', multiple: 'first', naMatches: 'never', suffix: ['x', '_y']);



# A tibble: 4 × 3
     id v.x   v.y  
  <int> <chr> <chr>
1     1 a     <NA> 
2     2 b     B    
3     2 b     B2   
4    NA c     C    
# A tibble: 3 × 3
     id vx    v_y  
  <int> <chr> <chr>
1     1 a     <NA> 
2     2 b     B    
3    NA c     <NA>
A row of x that matches several rows of y appears once per match, so a join can return more rows than x has. The result keeps x’s row order, with several matches in y’s order. Unmatched rows of x get NA in y’s columns in a left or full join. multiple: and relationship: limit or check the matches.
Joins keep x’s grouping, except for a grouping column that the join renames.

Rows of x with a match in y, with y’s columns.
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->innerJoin(). Example.

All rows of x, with y’s columns where they match (NA otherwise).
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->leftJoin(). Example.



right_join(Table $y, JoinBy|array|string|null $by = null, array $suffix = ['.x', '.y'], ?bool $keep = null, string $naMatches = 'na', string $multiple = 'all', string $unmatched = 'drop', ?string $relationship = null): Closure
All rows of y, with x’s columns where they match.
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->rightJoin().



full_join(Table $y, JoinBy|array|string|null $by = null, array $suffix = ['.x', '.y'], ?bool $keep = null, string $naMatches = 'na', string $multiple = 'all', ?string $relationship = null): Closure
All rows of both tables.
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->fullJoin(). Join two tables.



semi_join(Table $y, JoinBy|array|string|null $by = null, string $naMatches = 'na'): Closure
Rows of x that have a match in y (x’s columns only).
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->semiJoin().



anti_join(Table $y, JoinBy|array|string|null $by = null, string $naMatches = 'na'): Closure
Rows of x that have no match in y.
Returns a function of a table, which returns a table. Chain method: ->antiJoin(). Example.



cross_join(Table $y, array $suffix = ['.x', '.y']): Closure
Every combination of rows of x and y.

The join functions take the right-hand table as their first argument. The input table is the left-hand table x.

The options follow dplyr 1.1:

suffix: renames clashing non-key columns, ['.x', '.y'] by default.
keep: true keeps y’s key columns.
naMatches: 'never' stops NA keys from matching. By default NA matches NA.

title: Joins, binding, and set operations
text:
join_by()
join_by() builds dplyr’s join specifications. A string is an equality on the same column name, ['a' => 'b'] maps names, and a comparison of two col() expressions compares x’s column (left) with y’s (right). Every condition must hold.
join_by('id', col('t')->ge(col('start')), col('t')->lt(col('end')))
join_by('id', between('t', 'start', 'end'))        // start and end are y's columns
join_by('id', closest(col('t')->ge(col('start'))))  // the latest start at or before t
join_by(within('lo', 'hi', 'start', 'end'))         // x's interval inside y's
join_by(overlaps('lo', 'hi', 'start', 'end'))
For inequality, rolling, and overlap joins, keep defaults to dplyr’s behavior: equality keys are merged and the columns in other conditions are kept from both tables. keep: false is an error for these joins. Database tables run them in SQL, except right and full rolling joins, which load the rows.
nest_join() keeps every row of x and adds a list-column (name:, default 'data') holding each row’s matching rows of y as a table.

join_by()
join_by(mixed ...$conditions): JoinBy
A join specification, as dplyr’s join_by(). Conditions are column names (equality on the same name), [‘x’ => ‘y’] or [x, op, y] arrays, or comparisons where the left side is x’s column and the right side y’s:
join_by('id', col('t')->ge(col('start'))) join_by('id', between('t', 'start', 'end')) // bounds are y’s columns join_by(‘id’, closest(col('t')->ge(col('start')))) join_by(overlaps('start', 'end', 'from', 'to'))
Every condition must hold. Inequality and rolling joins keep the key columns of both tables, as in dplyr.
Returns JoinBy.


closest()
closest(mixed $condition): Closest
A rolling join: keep only the closest match, as in join_by(closest(col('t')->ge(col('start')))).
Returns Closest.


within()
within(string $xLower, string $xUpper, string $yLower, string $yUpper): array
x’s interval [xLower, xUpper] lies within y’s [yLower, yUpper].
Returns array.


overlaps()
overlaps(string $xLower, string $xUpper, string $yLower, string $yUpper): array
x’s interval [xLower, xUpper] overlaps y’s [yLower, yUpper].
Returns array.

title: Joins, binding, and set operations
Joins, binding, and set operations
text:
Set operations and row updates
union(), union_all(), intersect(), setdiff(), and symdiff() compare whole rows. setequal() returns true when both tables hold the same distinct rows.
The rows_*() functions modify the input table using another table’s rows, matched on by: (y’s first column by default):

rows_insert() adds rows with new keys; conflict: 'ignore' skips existing keys.
rows_append() adds all rows.
rows_update() overwrites values for matching keys.
rows_patch() fills only NA values for matching keys.
rows_upsert() updates matching keys and inserts new ones.
rows_delete() removes matching keys.

unmatched: 'ignore' allows y keys that x lacks.

PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


$stock = DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['sku' => 'A1', 'qty' => 5],
    ['sku' => 'B2', 'qty' => null],
    ['sku' => 'C3', 'qty' => 0],
]);
$delivery = DataFrame::fromRows([['sku' => 'B2', 'qty' => 12], ['sku' => 'D4', 'qty' => 3]]);

echo $stock |> rows_upsert($delivery, by: 'sku');
echo "\n", $stock |> rows_patch($delivery, by: 'sku', unmatched: 'ignore');
echo "\n", $stock |> setdiff(DataFrame::fromRows([['sku' => 'C3', 'qty' => 0]]));


$stock = DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['sku' => 'A1', 'qty' => 5],
    ['sku' => 'B2', 'qty' => null],
    ['sku' => 'C3', 'qty' => 0],
]);
$delivery = DataFrame::fromRows([['sku' => 'B2', 'qty' => 12], ['sku' => 'D4', 'qty' => 3]]);

echo phplyr($stock)->rowsUpsert($delivery, by: 'sku');
echo "\n", phplyr($stock)->rowsPatch($delivery, by: 'sku', unmatched: 'ignore');
echo "\n", phplyr($stock)->setdiff(DataFrame::fromRows([['sku' => 'C3', 'qty' => 0]]));
